items.explanation: 「静けさを必要としない職場は、アプリストアには並んでいない」 means a workplace that does not drive people to need calm must be built, not purchased, echoing 「世界を問うこと」. It is not about a gap in the app market, the power of meditation, or office architecture.

items.stem: What is the writer's main claim about the maxim 'history is written by the victors'?
choices: It is simply false, because in the Ugan case the defeated side actually wrote most of the official chronicle.
It shows that the conquerors' chronicle is worthless and should be replaced by temple and merchant records.
It implies that histories written to restore the voice of the defeated are generally more reliable than those written by the victors themselves.
It is a useful starting point, but taken as a conclusion it hides how texts were negotiated under specific conditions.
items.explanation: The writer calls the maxim 「出発点としては有効」 but warns that 「それを結論にしてしまえば、史料の襞に刻まれた複雑な交渉を見落とす」. Only 「一部」 of the chronicle may be by former retainers; the chronicle is to be read closely, not discarded; and restorative local histories are criticized.

items.stem: What does 「面従腹背」 suggest about the former Ugan retainers who wrote parts of the chronicle?
choices: They betrayed their former king in order to win office and favour under the conquering dynasty.
They openly resisted the conquerors by writing an alternative history of the kingdom that circulated in secret.
They outwardly served the new rulers' purposes while covertly preserving a record of their former lord.
They invented the story of the last king's tyranny to protect themselves from the new regime.
items.explanation: 面従腹背 means obeying on the surface while resisting inwardly, matching 「新しい主君の意向に沿いながらも、旧主の事績をひそかに書き留める」. They did not betray the king, resist openly, or fabricate his tyranny, which the text attributes to the victors' view.

items.stem: Why does the writer mention the recent trend in local history writing?
choices: To show that efforts to recover the defeated's voice can themselves serve aims other than accuracy.
To praise local historians for finally correcting the distortions of the conquerors' chronicle.
To demonstrate that the victors' view of Ugan still dominates the way the region is studied today.
To argue that the culture of the Ugan people was completely lost after their kingdom's fall.
items.explanation: The trend is said to lean 「実証よりも郷土の誇りの醸成に」, illustrating the second point that restorative history 「しばしば別の目的に奉仕する」. It is criticism, not praise; it shows a counter-view rather than victor dominance; and the text says the people kept their rites and language.

items.stem: What position does the editorial take?
choices: Predictive policing should be banned outright, since any use of past crime data will inevitably reproduce existing discrimination.
Without disclosure and outside review, predictive policing risks hardening past bias behind a look of objectivity.
Algorithms are more objective than officers' hunches, so they should gradually replace human judgment.
The prefecture's trial will fail mainly because ten years of records are too little data to train on.
items.explanation: The writer demands 「公開し、外部の検証を受ける仕組み」, warning otherwise of 「不公正を自動化するだけ」. A ban is explicitly rejected (「一律に禁じよとは言わない」); the objectivity claim is the proponents' view that the writer answers; data quantity is never the issue.

items.stem: What does the writer mean by saying the prediction 'produces the evidence that justifies itself'?
choices: The system fabricates crime records in districts where officers were not actually able to observe anything.
Residents of heavily patrolled districts commit more offences because constant surveillance provokes them.
Officers deliberately exaggerate their reports so that the algorithm will later justify larger patrol budgets for their own stations.
Sending more officers to flagged districts yields more recorded offences there, which seems to confirm the forecast.
items.explanation: The loop is: biased records → 「そこに一層多くの警察官を送り込めば、記録はさらに偏る」. Nothing says records are fabricated, that surveillance provokes crime, or that officers inflate reports on purpose.

items.stem: Why does the writer invoke the principle 「疑わしきは罰せず」?
choices: To warn that predictive policing will directly cause more innocent defendants to be wrongly convicted in the criminal courts.
To argue that it also implies not casting suspicion on people who have done nothing, merely because of probability.
To suggest that the principle is outdated in an age when crime can be forecast with statistical tools.
To argue that officers whose decisions reveal bias should themselves be disciplined and punished.
items.explanation: The writer reads the principle 「裏を返せば、何もしていない者をいたずらに疑いの眼差しにさらさないという約束」, against treating people 「行為ではなく可能性によって」. Wrongful convictions, obsolescence of the principle, and punishing officers are not argued.

items.stem: What does the keeper realize on 一月十五日 when rereading the logs?
choices: Though the logs record only facts, he senses they are filled with the feeling that went unwritten.
He regrets that his father and grandfather kept careless records that left out essential details.
He resolves that feelings have no place in a log and that he must keep his own entries strictly factual.
He discovers that his grandfather had in fact recorded private emotions between the weather reports.
items.explanation: He notes 「感情の類は一行もない」 yet feels 「書かれなかったものの方が、この帳面には多く詰まっている」. The logs are not called careless; he makes no resolution; and the grandfather's entries contain no emotions.

items.stem: What does the keeper finally conclude was the essence of his work?
choices: Maintaining the lamp with a care and precision that the new automatic machinery could never achieve.
Keeping accurate weather and shipping records so that the central office could manage the coast and its shipping lanes safely.
Continuing to believe that someone was out in the dark, even without knowing if the signal was received.
Preserving a family tradition of service that had been handed down through three generations.
items.explanation: The 三月三十日 entry states 「闇の中に誰かがいると信じ続けることであった」, prepared by the fog entry: 「届いたかどうかを知らされぬまま、合図を送り続ける」. He concedes the machine's light will be stronger; records and family are present but not named as the essence.

items.stem: What effect does the final entry, which returns to the stock phrase 「記録すべき事項、以上」, create?
choices: Restraint that masks, and thereby underlines, the weight of the last night the light is tended.
Relief that a lonely and burdensome duty has at last come to an end after so many years.
Indifference, showing he has accepted automation as something that does not affect him at all.
Barely suppressed anger at the central office for closing a lighthouse his family had kept.
items.explanation: After the confession of 三月三十日, the return to the formula mirrors the 'nothing but facts' tradition, so emotion is conveyed by what is left unsaid. The text shows no relief or anger, and the ironic 「結構なことである」 and the solitary bow on New Year's Eve contradict indifference.

items.stem: What conclusion does the writer reach?
choices: The non-identity problem shows that, strictly speaking, present policies cannot wrong any particular person who happens to be born in the future.
A trustee ethic of handing on what we inherited should replace cost-benefit analysis as the basis of climate policy.
Discounting future harm is justified, since future generations can be expected to be wealthier than people are today.
The puzzles do not cancel our duties to future people but call for combining several moral intuitions rather than one framework.
items.explanation: The writer says 「これらの難問は、将来世代への配慮を放棄する理由にはならない」 and recommends 「複数の倫理的直観を重ね合わせる」 without 「いずれか一つを絶対視」. The non-identity argument is presented as a challenge, not accepted; the trustee ethic is said to 「揺れる」; the wealth argument is rebutted.

items.stem: What is the writer's objection to the argument used to support discounting?
choices: It relies on discount rates that are mathematically incoherent when applied over a hundred years.
It overvalues distant damages and so leads to excessive spending on climate policy today.
It assumes that future people will be richer, which is exactly what climate change puts in doubt.
It ignores the fact that future generations cannot vote on the policies that affect them.
items.explanation: The text: the forecast of future wealth 「は気候変動がまさに脅かしている前提そのものである」. The writer does not call the maths incoherent, says discounting undervalues (not overvalues) future harm, and treats voting under a separate point.

items.stem: What worry does the writer raise under the third point, 'representation'?
choices: Future generations will probably reject the climate policies that the present generation adopts.
Those who speak for future generations may simply be projecting their own present values onto them.
Representatives of future generations are chosen by processes that are not properly democratic.
International negotiations tend to exclude the countries that will suffer most from climate change.
items.explanation: The key sentence is 「その代弁者が、実のところ自らの価値観を未来に投影しているにすぎない可能性」. Future rejection, how representatives are chosen, and exclusion of particular countries are not discussed.

items.stem: What does the writer mean by 「書かれていないことこそが、この手紙の本文であった」?
choices: The aunt hid her illness because she did not trust the writer and wished to keep her distance from the family.
The aunt's silence about her illness, shown through unsteady writing and long talk of flowers, was the real message.
The letter was left unfinished, and the writer only later understood what the missing part would have said.
The writer later found a second page that openly described the diagnosis and treatment the aunt had received that same week.
items.explanation: Written 「入院を告げられた翌週」, the letter never mentions illness, but the 「筆跡がところどころ乱れ」 and flowers that bloom, fall and will bloom next year carry it. Distrust, an unfinished letter, and a second page are not in the text.

items.stem: What is the writer's attitude toward modern instant messaging?
choices: It is granted to be efficient and even honest, yet it leaves no room for what cannot be put into words.
It is dismissed as shallow and dishonest, a clear decline from the sincerity of handwritten letters.
It is to be resisted, and the writer urges readers to return to the habit of writing letters by hand.
It is welcomed without reservation, since removing ambiguity finally frees people from misunderstanding.
items.explanation: The writer calls it 「効率的で、ある意味では誠実ですらある」 but asks whether saying everything 「言葉にならないものの居場所を奪う」. The writer refuses to 「声高に言う」 a return to letters and warns against 「懐古趣味」, so neither dismissal nor unreserved welcome fits.

items.stem: What is the point of 「言外の意を察しろというのは、ときに受け手への横暴でもあった」?
choices: It criticizes people today who reply rudely and too quickly to messages sent by their elders.
It suggests that the aunt was a demanding correspondent who expected the writer to read her mind.
It argues that stating one's intentions plainly is itself a kind of tyranny over the reader.
It concedes that expecting others to infer unstated meaning could place an unfair burden on them.
items.explanation: The sentence explains why explicitness is 「誠実ですらある」: demanding that the reader 'read the air' could be 横暴 (high-handed) toward them. It does not criticize modern users, the aunt, or explicitness; the tyranny lies in the opposite habit.

items.stem: What does the editorial propose?
choices: Place the central bank under the direct control of the government, since it now makes inherently political choices.
Accept the bank's broad powers as legitimate, because it acts within the limits of a law duly passed by the national legislature.
Keep central bank independence but redraw its limits and require accountability for policies with distributional effects.
End the policy of near-zero interest rates, because it has widened inequality and damaged regional banks.
items.explanation: The writer calls for 「独立性を維持しつつ、その範囲を改めて画定し直すこと」 plus 「事前説明と事後検証」. Government control is rejected as 「角を矯めて牛を殺す愚」; the legal argument is only 「形式論として」 correct; and ending zero rates is not proposed.

items.stem: In context, what does 「角を矯めて牛を殺す」 warn against?
choices: Allowing large-scale asset purchases to continue until they undermine the pension funds and regional banks they affect.
Abolishing independence to fix its legitimacy problem, thereby destroying the protection that independence provides.
Letting politicians inflate the currency for short-term gains at the expense of long-term price stability.
Leaving a small gap in the central bank law that eventually ruins the credibility of the whole institution.
items.explanation: The idiom means ruining the whole while correcting a small flaw; the 'flaw' is the legitimacy deficit and the 'ox' is the protection of 「通貨の番人を政治から守る必要」. The other options name real concerns in the passage but not the one this idiom targets.

items.stem: Why does the writer mention Odysseus binding himself to the mast?
choices: To illustrate the classic rationale of independence as a precommitment against a foreseeable temptation to inflate.
To suggest that central bankers are heroic figures who resist pressures ordinary politicians cannot withstand.
To warn that unelected experts may themselves be seduced by power once they are freed from elections.
To show that binding rules have historically failed and that discretion must be left to the central bank.
items.explanation: The image is introduced as a summary of 「独立性を支える古典的な論理」: politicians 「通貨を膨張させる誘惑に抗いがたい」, so they tie their own hands. It does not glorify bankers, warn about their seduction, or argue against rules.

items.stem: What is the writer's central argument?
choices: Irony should be abandoned, since those in power have taken it over and now use it against their critics.
Irony has always been, and still remains, a weapon that only the weak can use against the powerful.
Irony's worth depends on who aims it at whom; it now also shields the powerful and breeds cynicism.
Direct accusation is a more effective way to criticize power than irony has ever been in any era.
items.explanation: The writer concludes 「問われているのは、誰が、誰に向けて、それを用いているかである」 after describing irony as 「隠れ蓑」 and a path to 「虚無」. Giving it up is rejected (「そうではあるまい」); the politician example shows it is no longer only the weak's weapon; and the sword is not ranked above the mirror.

items.stem: How does the politician's retort 'can't you take a joke?' work, according to the writer?
choices: It reveals that the politician genuinely meant the remark as harmless humour that critics misread.
It is a form of self-mockery that disarms critics by showing the politician can laugh at himself.
It is a pointed satire of the critics themselves that exposes the hypocrisy hidden behind their loud public outrage.
It exploits irony's deniability: supporters hear the remark as sincere, while critics are cast as humourless.
items.explanation: The text: 「本気で受け取った者には本気として届き、批判する者には…野暮という烙印」, because 「言ったことを言わなかったことにできる」. The writer does not accept the joke as genuine, and nothing suggests self-mockery or exposure of critics' hypocrisy.

items.stem: What does 「下に向けられた鏡」 refer to?
choices: Self-criticism by satirists who turn their irony against their own side and their own habits.
Irony so subtle that ordinary readers fail to notice the criticism hidden in its surface praise.
Censorship that forces critics to aim their satire at harmless targets instead of the powerful.
Irony directed at weaker people, which only mocks and distorts them instead of exposing power.
items.explanation: The mirror metaphor was introduced for irony reflecting power back on itself; aimed downward it 「ただ弱い者の姿を歪めて映すだけ」. It is not about self-criticism, over-subtlety, or censorship.

items.stem: What does the writer see as the root of the crisis in craft transmission?
choices: The government's video archive is wasteful, and its budget should go instead to paying the remaining masters.
Because masters cannot explain their skills, far better motion analysis is needed to put the craft fully into words and numbers.
Society no longer supports the long apprenticeship through which tacit skill is absorbed; recording cannot replace it.
Young people today lack the patience to endure the years of hardship that an apprenticeship demands.
items.explanation: The writer says 「問題の根は、その時間を誰も買えなくなったことにある」 and that records must be joined by society taking on 「修業の時間そのもの」. The writer does not deny the archive's value, doubts that analysis can capture the judgment, and blames income and prospects, not youth.

items.stem: How does the writer reinterpret the proverb 「石の上にも三年」?
choices: As a plain statement of how long it takes knowledge to settle into the body, not as a moral about endurance.
As praise for the virtue of perseverance, which the writer thinks today's apprentices sorely need.
As a criticism of traditional apprenticeships that waste years before trainees learn anything useful.
As evidence that three years is enough to master a craft if the training is organized efficiently.
items.explanation: The text: 「忍耐の美徳を説いているのではない。知が身体に沈殿するのに要する時間を、率直に述べている」. The other readings either restore the moral reading the writer rejects or add claims about waste or sufficiency that are absent.

items.stem: What does the writer mean by calling video records 「標本」?
choices: They capture a craft more precisely than any master could, and so are more valuable than living teachers.
They preserve the outward form of a craft but cannot by themselves bring new living practitioners into being.
They show that the craft is already dead, so all the remaining effort should go into public museums and archives.
They are useful only to scholars studying the craft, not to the apprentices who hope to practise it.
items.explanation: 「標本は生き物の姿を後世に伝えるが、標本から生き物は生まれない」: a specimen keeps the shape but cannot reproduce life. The writer does not rank records above masters, declare the craft dead, or limit records to scholars.

items.stem: What is the writer's main argument?
choices: The ideal of wa is outdated and should be discarded by companies that wish to compete successfully in today's global economy.
Japanese firms owe their postwar success to an ancient culture of harmony that is now in danger of vanishing.
Lifetime employment and seniority pay are the direct causes of the scandals that have hit Japanese firms.
The popular notion of wa as conformity distorts its origins and history, and it serves those who silence dissent.
items.explanation: The writer argues the myth 「過去を編集する」, that wa meant 「異論を戦わせた後の調和」, and that 「和を乱すな」 is a tool 「異論を封じる」. The writer explicitly says 「和そのものを捨てよと言うのではない」, rejects the ancient-culture story, and does not blame employment practices for scandals.

items.stem: According to the writer, what did the ancient phrase originally mean?
choices: That when superiors and subordinates discuss things amicably, reason will naturally prevail.
That subordinates should keep their objections to themselves out of loyalty to their superiors.
That any open conflict must be avoided, even at the price of leaving problems unresolved.
That the group must always be placed ahead of the individual in every public matter.
items.explanation: The text glosses it as 「上下の者が睦まじく論じ合えば道理は自ずから通る」, not 「議論を封じて同調を強いること」. The other three describe the modern corporate misreading that the writer criticizes.

items.stem: Why does the writer mention labour conditions in prewar factories?
choices: To argue that labour relations before the war were healthier because workers could openly dispute.
To show that frequent job changes before the war were what later produced lifetime employment.
To show that 'wa management' practices are fairly recent products of postwar conditions, not an ancient trait.
To suggest that labour disputes, rather than harmony, were the real source of Japan's rapid postwar economic growth.
items.explanation: High turnover and frequent disputes before the war show that long-term employment arose from 「戦後の労働力不足や労使交渉の帰結」, 「太古から続く国民性の発露などではない」. The writer neither praises prewar relations nor credits disputes with growth, and turnover is not named as the cause.

items.stem: What does the final phrase 「沈黙の共謀」 convey?
choices: Employees who say nothing in meetings are secretly plotting together against their managers.
Harmony kept by staying silent is really a shared complicity in avoiding uncomfortable truths.
Silence in meetings is a respectful form of agreement that foreign observers fail to grasp.
Foreign management writers have conspired to spread a flattering myth about Japanese firms.
items.explanation: After 「口をつぐんで保たれる和は、和ではなく」, the phrase labels such silence as collusion in letting problems (like unheeded warnings) go unaddressed. It is not literal plotting, a defence of silence, or a conspiracy by foreign authors.

items.stem: Where, according to the writer, does the real value of science fiction lie?
choices: In predicting accurately which technologies and social systems will emerge in the future.
In escaping censorship, which is why it flourishes chiefly under authoritarian governments.
In offering thrilling entertainment that lets readers forget the troubles of their daily lives for a while.
In estranging the present so that readers can no longer see their own world in the same way.
items.explanation: The last sentence: 「真価は、未来を当てることではなく、現在を見知らぬものに変えることにある」. Prediction is explicitly denied; escaping censorship is one effect, not the essence; and entertainment is what dystopia degrades into, which the writer treats as a risk.

items.stem: Why does the writer describe a Mars colony where oxygen rations determine class?
choices: To predict that future space colonies will be organized around unequal access to scarce resources.
To mock the cliched settings of science fiction that keep it from being taken seriously as literature.
To show how an invented setting lets readers recognize injustice in how their own society shares out necessities.
To show that readers prefer exotic adventure to realistic stories about their everyday lives.
items.explanation: Readers, outraged by the colony, 「酸素を水や住居や教育に置き換えてみて、慄然とする」, illustrating 「異化」. The example is not a forecast, not mockery of clichés, and not about readers' taste for adventure.

items.stem: What does the writer imply by saying that stories condemning surveillance societies 'sell well within surveillance societies'?
choices: Science fiction has succeeded in changing society, since its warnings now reach a mass readership.
Social critique can be defused into entertainment and consumed within the very system it condemns.
Publishers in controlled societies deliberately promote dystopias in order to distract their readers.
Readers usually misunderstand dystopian novels and take them to be praise of the regimes they depict.
items.explanation: The sentence follows 「ディストピアは、消費されるうちに、恐怖の対象から一種の娯楽へと変わってしまう」 and is called 「皮肉」. Wide sales are not presented as social change, and there is no claim about deliberate promotion or misreading as praise.
